title: The Belém Call: Mobilizing Finance for Forest Protection
description: Join us today for a webinar exploring the Belém Call to Action for the Congo Basin Forests, a landmark initiative launched at COP30 that mobilizes over USD 2.5 billion to halt and reverse deforestation by 2030. The Congo Basin—home to the world’s second-largest tropical rainforest—plays a vital role in global climate regulation, biodiversity, and local livelihoods. This session will unpack the Call’s objectives, financing, and alignment with the Congo Basin Forest Partnership roadmap, and discuss what it means in practice for governments, Indigenous Peoples, local communities, and partners working to turn this commitment into lasting impact.

title: Why are organisational financial capacities crucial for tenure rights?
description:
The climate and biodiversity crises have forced the world to pledge billions of dollars to mitigate the impact of environmental degradation, a significant portion of which should be heading for Indigenous Peoples, Afro-descedant and local communities as they have sustained their own communities and forests for generations.  

As long-term partners with Indigenous Peoples, Afro-descendant and local community organisations’ Tenure Facility has listened deeply to their needs. Overtime, they have shown us their keen interest to learn ‘conventional’ ways of handling finances to better protect their space, as securing their land and forest rights requires substantial financial resources and stable financial systems.

In 2024, Tenure Facility, with the support of Spring Strategies, kickstarted the Financial Training Programme to provide partners in Latin America with effective finance and administrative tools, strengthened financial capacities to enable them to acquire more funds, and guidance in the implementation of their plans.

title: Gender and biodiversity: How Indigenous and Local Community Women Safeguard Nature - Land Dialogue
description:
Indigenous women's knowledge is rooted in a deep appreciation of the natural world. They possess an intricate understanding of various species, their nutritional value, medicinal properties, and ecological roles. This knowledge passed down through generations, not only enriches their communities but has been crucial for science.

Despite this, Indigenous women often remain marginalised and relegated to the status of beneficiaries rather than recognised as partners and agents of change.

As we look forward to COP16 and discussions surrounding the Global Biodiversity Framework, amplifying their voices and integrating their perspectives into global dialogues on benefit-sharing and biodiversity conservation becomes increasingly important.

Hear from Indigenous leaders on how to best support and recognise women as the custodians of traditional knowledge systems.

title: Who We Are
description:
Providing funding when and where it is needed: 

Tenure Facility is the leading financial mechanism specialised in supporting Indigenous Peoples and local communities to secure and sustain their land and their forest rights. We work directly with partners to provide targeted funding, along with technical assistance, to help achieve their vision through tailored projects. These efforts benefit our shared planet as well – by reducing deforestation, cutting carbon emissions, restoring ecosystems, and promoting human rights. 

While primarily a financial mechanism, Tenure Facility also works with its partners to support gender equality and encourage youth involvement, and local governance. Along with mapping, learning events, and other areas of engagement, these collaborative initiatives reduce conflict and create a vibrant community of practice.

title: Leading the Way: How Indigenous Youth Combat Climate Change Through Land Rights
description:
Young Indigenous Peoples are facing unprecedented challenges as they grow up in a world where climate change imperils their community’s cultural heritage and ways of life. In response, many are becoming new leaders in climate activism, championing land rights as a pivotal measure in combating environmental degradation and preserving traditional lifestyles.

Our first Land Dialogue of 2024 explores the dynamic relationship between land tenure systems and climate resilience through the lens of Indigenous Peoples and local community youth. In a rapidly urbanizing world and warming, we will examine how youth are being encouraged to embrace their ancestral knowledge systems, the nature-based solutions that are being widely applauded, to defend their land and territories and actively lead on climate change.

Our discussion will focus on solutions and highlight youth-led responses to land and climate issues. Moreover, the webinar will provide a space for cross-cultural learning between young people worldwide, sparking unlikely but meaningful conversations. Listen in as young leaders create a space for a new kind of dialogue where Indigenous youth lead the way.

title: Inter-State Movement of Babassu Coconut Breakers in  Piauí
description:
Vila Esperança, State of Piauí, Brazil, our partner, the Inter-State Movement of Babassu Coconut Breakers, promotes the implementation of 3 state and 18 municipal “free babassu” laws, which protect babassu palms and give women the right to harvest them anywhere.

🇧🇷Securing the boundaries and safeguarding the ancestral lands of Indigenous Peoples, Quilombolas, and local communities, while upholding the laws, ensuring free access to babassu palms for communities, or protecting forests from destruction, is not merely a matter of respecting tenure rights - it is the cornerstone of effective conservation in the Brazilian Amazon. 

🌎 Strong tenure rights protect traditional forest guardianship, which is pivotal in combatting climate change. By entrusting forests to community management, we fortify their role as powerful stewards making a significant positive impact on the planet's climate.

title: Climate Funding and COP28 : Turning Pledges into Action
description:
The UN’s past two global climate summits have been big on promises for Indigenous Peoples. At COP26 in 2021 governments and private philanthropies pledged nearly $2 billion for Indigenous Peoples and local communities to fight deforestation. Last year’s COP27 led to the creation of a new “loss and damage” fund to help vulnerable communities respond to climate disasters. Leaders are now again preparing for a round of climate talks at COP28, which start later this month in Dubai, this time vowing to enhance the participation and visibility of Indigenous Peoples during the negotiations.  

But why has the follow through been so tough? Promises to support and fund Indigenous Peoples are falling short so what is standing in the way of progress and who (or what) is needed to kickstart investments? And how could newly established Indigenous-led funds lead the way forward? 

This webinar will gather experts and on-the-ground activists to examine how commitments from past COPs to Indigenous Peoples and local communities have not filtered down to where they matter most as well as how this year’s summit can fix climate financing by making it more inclusive and responsive to these communities and their own funding mechanisms. The session will also highlight the importance of robust data in monitoring and tracking climate funds set aside for Indigenous Peoples and local communities.

Indigenous Peoples have an outsized role in addressing climate change, and have unique perspectives and needs that should be considered in the lead-up to COP28. However, many communities wouldn’t be able to carry out concrete solutions unless delegates at COP28 ensure that the financial pledges and commitments are honoured.

description:

description:
The Asia Regional Learning Exchange was one of three regional learning exchanges planned for 2023-2024, as an important part of our commitment to create opportunities for partners to meet, share and learn from each other.

Sharing knowledge helps others learn, fosters collaboration and reinforces our own understanding. That’s exactly what partners of the Tenure Facility, International Land Coalition, the Samdhana Institute and the Indonesian Coalition for Tenure Justice did in June at our first regional learning exchange of 2023. 

The five-day event united more than 120 participants from nine countries across Asia in Bali, Indonesia, to exchange ideas and personal experiences from Indigenous Peoples and local communities.

title: Rapid deforestation of the Amazon could influence temperatures over the Tibetan plateau
description:
📃From New Scientist : Saini Yang at Beijing Normal University in China and her colleagues analysed global climatological data from 1979 to 2019 to identify correlations in temperature and precipitation between the Amazon rainforest and other areas. Such links are called “teleconnections”.

❗️They focused on the Amazon rainforest in particular because of its significance as a major carbon sink and as a climatic “tipping point” that could see forest turn to savannah beyond a certain threshold of warming and human-driven deforestation. 

🔥The researchers found that since 1979, warm temperatures in the Amazon correlated with warm temperatures over the Tibetan plateau and the West Antarctic ice sheet; more precipitation in the Amazon was associated with less precipitation in those regions.

📉By analysing changing temperatures in the regions between the Amazon and those distant areas, they were also able to trace the path through which energy or materials such as black carbon released in forest fires might propagate through the atmosphere.

title: Lessons in climate resilience: what can we learn from indigenous and local communities?
description:
Indigenous Peoples globally have high exposure to environmental change and are often considered an ‘‘at-risk’’ population, although there is growing evidence of their resilience. Ample research illustrates that Indigenous Peoples are actively observing and adapting to change in a diversity of ways. In this webinar we will examine the common factor affecting resilience to environmental change among Indigenous Peoples and local communities.

The concept of resilience has been outlined and used in different ways and we use it here to think holistically about the general characteristics that affect the ‘‘capacity of individuals, communities, and systems to survive, adapt, and grow in the face of stress and shocks, and even transform when conditions require it.” Strong connections to the land heldby many indigenous and local communities bring unique reflections for understanding and responding to environmental change. Thus, the indirect effects of environmental change on interpersonal and environmental relationships, life experience, belief systems, family, and oral history are often as important as, if not more so, the more direct impacts of climate change.

description:
The COVID-19 pandemic has shed light on the imbalance in ecosystems being driven by human activities, and the urgent need for us to take action for the future of all species, including mankind. To do this, this webinar will highlight the support these communities need to continue their work protecting their territories.

title: Indigenous Peoples forests governance: a fundamental strategy
description: This webinar provided an opportunity to review the report “Forest Governance by Indigenous and Tribal Peoples” by FAO and FILAC, and its main arguments. It will discuss how governments can move forward formal recognition of territorial rights to indigenous and tribal territories and their forests that have yet to receive such recognition while reaching agreement with Indigenous and tribal traditional authorities about rules related to territorial planning and forest management, as well as coordinate actions to ensure those rules are respected. It will also debate how global and national plans for preventing deforestation, forest degradation and carbon emissions on Indigenous and tribal territories should ensure safe living conditions and channel new investments to support traditional livelihoods.

title: Rolling back social and environmental safeguards in the name of COVID-19 Recorded Webinar
description:
Global leaders increasingly recognise that land rights for indigenous and local communities are a prerequisite for achieving national and international goals for forest governance, food security, climate mitigation, economic development and human rights.

In 2020, however, the COVID-19 pandemic shifted the political context in many countries, and some governments used the pandemic as a justification for dismantling the protections gained by Indigenous and Forest Peoples. This has been particularly common in heavily forested countries where there are large indigenous communities. In this webinar, experts talked about how the roll back has affected safeguards, particularly in these five country-specific reports on Brazil, Colombia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Indonesia, and Perú. These reports address the following question: Since the outbreak of COVID-19, to what extent are the five most tropically forested countries rolling back social and environmental safeguards and if so, what are, or may be, the negative consequences in terms of land grabs, rights abuse and deforestation in indigenous territories.

title: Stories of resilience- Peru
description: In Peru, the work to right historic wrongs against Indigenous Peoples, has been strengthened in the last years. Last year, the Peruvian President himself attended an emotional ceremony in the vast northern Loreto region to see 66 indigenous communities receive the title to their lands. But with the country been badly hit by the coronavirus, Indigenous populations are seeing resurgent threats to their lands, livelihoods and lives. During Coronavirus, the local authorities are doing what they can to provide assistance, but still, many communities are turning to traditional medicines. The pandemic has allowed Tenure Facility’s partners to reflect on the relevance of the issues at stake. The silver lining during this pandemic has been the government pursue of an ambitious plan to recognize the lands of all identified indigenous and peasant communities by 2021.

title: Stories of resilience- Panama
description: Panama has some of the world’s most progressive laws protecting indigenous rights. Yet in recent years pressure has been growing on the county’s indigenous Peoples - from the private sector, the landless poor, and the Government’s claims to protected areas. Nevertheless, Indigenous Peoples are uniting once more and building their capacity, making them a serious force to be reckoned with. An example of this, has been now with the pandemic, traditional practices have become central to their response. Many Indigenous Peoples have turned to traditional medicines to mitigate the impacts of the virus. While no one is suggesting that these medicines offer a cure to COVID-19, there use is a reminder of the extraordinary wisdom residing in indigenous cultures

title: Stories of resilience- Nepal
description:
After a decade of political upheaval, Nepal entered a phase of peace process and
stability which brought with it a new constitution that saw land reforms and tenure rights properly established in law. However, efforts to digitise land registration remain patchy. The legal rights of community forestry groups can be withdrawn at any time by forestry officials. This situation has been worsened by the arrival of the pandemic; however, the Tenure facility’s partners have been working to coordinate with the local communities and carry on with the project in the best way they can.

title: Stories of resilience- Mozambique
description: Land tenure has always been a source of friction in Mozambique, however Mozambique has developed some of the best policies and legal frameworks for land tenure on the African continent. Nevertheless, most rural farmers are unable to obtain documentation that proves the existence of their land rights. Now with the pandemic, restricted movement between rural and urban areas has fuelled a collapse in the socio-economic system in the country. Despite there being few if any reported cases of COVID-19 in the communities where our partners are working, the impact has been felt and seen in the country. Everyone recognises the importance of finding ways to work in a world that has altered and may remain altered for a long time to come.

title: Stories of resilience- Liberia
description: After decades of conflict over land which helped fuel a bitter civil war, in 2018 a new land law was passed in Liberia which meant that rural communities had the chance to gain greater control over their ancestral lands. The Tenure Facility backed project has placed the role of women at the heart of strengthening the capacity of these communities to title and manage their lands. But the arrival of COVID-19 has created severe challenges. Deadly diseases are nothing new in Liberia, but lockdown rules have left rural families short of vital food and medicine, and economic pressures have seen an ominous rise in sexual and gender-based violence. Nonetheless, our partners have been relying on the expertise they gained during the Ebola crisis to confront COVID-19 and its challenges to bring forward a brighter future.

title: Stories of resilience- Democratic Republic of Congo
description:
DRC:
Early in 2020 our partners were busy preparing for the June launch of the Tenure Facility-backed project, which will see communities being supported to make use of a new ministerial order on communal lands to secure 300,000 hectares of forestlands in western DRC. With the arrival of the pandemic however, already isolated villages found themselves more cut off than ever through lock down. Already impoverished communities have gone hungry, and whilst there has been little spread of the virus itself, fear of its impacts has proved to be an infection of its own. Despite this, our partners have shown resilience and adaptability to these changing circumstances while moving forward.

title: Stewards of the planet  Indigenous Peoples’ and local communities’ land and forest rights & climate
description:
Over half the world’s land is customarily claimed by Indigenous Peoples and local communities- yet they have legal ownership to less than 10 percent. This means people who have often lived on, relied on and protected their territories for generations can do little when powerful actors come to take it from them or destroy it. This has negative consequences far beyond the communities themselves: the lands in question are often some of the world’s last great forests, vital for planet health and the fight against climate change. 
Research shows that community land rights lead to lower deforestation rates, higher carbon storage and higher biodiversity. title: This is why the Tenure matters
description: One of our oldest instinctual parts of our brains is the need of building a home. But for the world's 2.5 billion Indigenous Peoples and local communities, land means so much more. It is their main source of their cultures and livelihoods. Their land and forests provide them with food, medicine and shelter. When they lose their homes their very way of life is threatened.
